subject: English
description: Tricky cases — collective nouns, either/or, neither/nor, indefinite pronouns, intervening phrases

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The committee ___ on the proposal next week.'

options.option_text: are deciding
is deciding
have decided
were decided

questions.explanation: COLLECTIVE NOUNS like committee, government, jury, team take SINGULAR verb when acting as a unit; PLURAL when members act individually. Here 'committee' acts as a unit → singular 'is deciding'. Distractor 1 — plural 'are' would be valid only if members are acting individually. Distractor 3 — 'have' is plural. Distractor 4 — 'were' is plural and 'decided' would be passive past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Neither the manager nor the staff ___ ready for the inspection.'

options.option_text: is
are
has
have been

questions.explanation: RULE: With 'either/or' and 'neither/nor', the verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST to it (the proximity rule). Here 'staff' (treated as plural) is nearest → plural verb 'are'. If reversed: 'Neither the staff nor the manager IS ready' would use singular. Distractor 1 — 'is' would match 'manager' (further from verb), wrong. Distractors 3, 4 — wrong tense/aspect.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Each of the players ___ given a uniform.'

options.option_text: are
is
have been
were

questions.explanation: RULE: 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither', 'none', 'one' are SINGULAR — take a singular verb, even when followed by a plural noun. 'Each of the players IS given'. Distractor 1 'are' is the common mistake (eyes track 'players'). Distractor 3 'have been' is plural. Distractor 4 'were' is plural past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The teacher, along with her students, ___ visiting the museum.'

options.option_text: are
is
have been
were

questions.explanation: Phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'in addition to', 'including' do NOT change the number of the subject. Subject = 'teacher' (singular) → singular verb 'is'. Compare with 'and' which DOES create a plural compound subject. Distractor 1 'are' wrongly responds to 'students'. Distractor 3 'have been' is plural. Distractor 4 'were' is plural past.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'A pair of shoes ___ kept in the wardrobe.'

options.option_text: are
is
has been
have

questions.explanation: 'Pair of' is grammatically singular as the subject (pair = one set of two items). 'A pair of shoes IS kept'. Similarly: 'a couple of friends' (singular when treating couple as unit). Distractor 1 'are' tracks 'shoes' but shoes is the OBJECT of 'of'. Distractor 3 — also passive but uses 'has been', incorrect with 'kept'. Distractor 4 'have' is plural.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'The number of accidents on this highway ___ rising every year.'

options.option_text: are
is
have been
were

questions.explanation: 'THE number of' — singular (refers to one specific count). Takes singular verb. CONTRAST: 'A number of' — plural (means 'several/many'). Examples: 'The number of cars IS rising' vs 'A number of cars ARE parked'. Distractor 1 'are' would be correct only with 'a number of'. Distractors 3, 4 are plural / wrong tense.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Mathematics ___ my favourite subject in school.'

options.option_text: are
is
have always been
were

questions.explanation: Subject names ending in -s — Mathematics, Physics, Statistics, Economics, Politics, News, Measles — are GRAMMATICALLY SINGULAR despite the -s ending. 'Mathematics is fascinating'. CONTRAST: 'his politics are confusing' (politics as views/opinions, not subject). Distractor 1 'are' wrongly treats 'mathematics' as plural. Distractors 3, 4 are also plural/wrong.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses the CORRECT verb form?

options.option_text: A number of complaints has been filed against the officer.
A number of complaints have been filed against the officer.
A number of complaints are filing against the local officer.
A number of complaints was filed against the officer yesterday.

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'a number of' means 'many' and acts as a plural quantifier, requiring a plural verb ('have been'). Option A is the prime distractor — learners confuse it with 'the number of', which is singular: 'the number of complaints is rising' is correct. 'A number of + plural noun' always takes a plural verb.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence in which the gerund subject agrees CORRECTLY with its verb.

options.option_text: Swimming in the ocean daily are considered a healthy habit.
Running marathons regularly help build stamina and endurance.
Reading books every evening improve your vocabulary greatly.
Walking briskly for thirty minutes burns significant calories.

questions.explanation: D is correct because a gerund phrase ('walking briskly for thirty minutes') acts as a singular noun-subject and requires a singular verb ('burns'). Options A, B, and C all use plural verbs ('are', 'help', 'improve') — the trap is the plural noun embedded in the phrase ('marathons', 'books') which misleads candidates into picking a plural verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence CORRECTLY applies the proximity rule for 'either…or' constructions?

options.option_text: Either the captain or the crew members is responsible for navigation.
Either the crew members or the captain is responsible for navigation.
Either the coach or the athletes was present at the morning briefing.
Either the teachers or the principal are responsible for school policy.

questions.explanation: B is correct: with 'either…or', the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it. Here 'the captain' (singular) is nearer, so 'is' is correct. Option A reverses the order — 'crew members' is nearer yet uses singular 'is'. Option D places 'principal' (singular) nearest but incorrectly uses 'are'. Option C places 'athletes' (plural) nearest but uses singular 'was'.

questions.stem: Select the sentence where the subject and verb are in CORRECT agreement.

options.option_text: The information shared at the meeting were not very reliable data.
The news about the recent floods have reached the district collector.
The advice given by the senior advocates was perfectly sound advice.
The luggage of all the passengers were checked thoroughly at the gate.

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'advice' is an uncountable noun and always requires a singular verb ('was'). Options A, B, and D use plural verbs ('were', 'have', 'were') with uncountable nouns 'information', 'news', and 'luggage' — a classic exam trap where prepositional phrases like 'of all the passengers' follow the head noun and make the subject appear plural.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with CORRECT subject-verb agreement involving an indefinite pronoun.

options.option_text: Everybody in the two neighbouring districts are aware of the policy.
Everyone attending the seminar were given a certificate of merit.
Somebody among the fifty applicants have submitted a false document.
Nobody in the three departments has submitted the required documents.

questions.explanation: D is correct: indefinite pronouns ending in '-body' and '-one' (everybody, everyone, somebody, nobody) are grammatically singular and require singular verbs — 'Nobody…has' is correct. Options A, B, C use plural verbs ('are', 'were', 'have'). The trap is the plural prepositional phrase following the pronoun ('in the two districts', 'among the fifty applicants') which candidates mistakenly treat as the subject.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence with CORRECT subject-verb agreement in the 'one of those who' construction.

options.option_text: He is one of those administrators who has reformed the system notably.
She is one of those athletes who have broken multiple national records.
This is one of those situations that demands immediate state attention.
He is one of those leaders who delivers results under extreme pressure.

questions.explanation: B is correct: in 'one of those [plural noun] who/that', the relative pronoun refers to the PLURAL NOUN ('athletes'), not to 'one'. The relative-clause verb must therefore be plural: 'have broken'. Options A, C, D all make the relative-clause verb singular ('has', 'demands', 'delivers') — the classic high-difficulty error where 'one' appears to be the controlling subject but is not.

questions.stem: Which sentence CORRECTLY applies the proximity rule for 'not only…but also' constructions?

options.option_text: Not only the Finance Minister but also the state heads is accountable.
Not only the state heads but also the Prime Minister are responsible.
Not only the warden but also the residents are required to attend.
Not only the residents but also the warden have to sign the register.

questions.explanation: C is correct: with 'not only…but also', the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it. 'The residents' (plural) is nearest, so 'are' is correct. Option B places 'the Prime Minister' (singular) nearest but uses plural 'are'. Option D places 'the warden' (singular) nearest but uses plural 'have'. Option A uses singular 'is' despite 'state heads' (plural) being nearest — all three represent distinct proximity-rule errors.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Many a young professional ___ to the city every year in search of better career opportunities'?

options.option_text: move — plural verb agreeing with 'many'
moves — singular verb, as 'many a' always takes singular
are moving — plural progressive incorrectly used here
have moved — plural perfect tense, grammatically wrong here

questions.explanation: 'Many a' is a fixed construction that always takes a singular noun and a singular verb. So 'many a young professional moves' is correct. Option A ('move') is the classic trap — students confuse 'many a' with plain 'many', which is plural and takes a plural verb. The two constructions are distinct rules.

questions.stem: Select the correct verb form: 'Among the documents submitted for verification ___ a forged certificate and two fake affidavits'?

options.option_text: was — singular verb treating only the first item as subject
were — plural verb for the compound subject after inversion
is being — present progressive, wrong tense and wrong number
had been — past perfect lacking a prior reference point here

questions.explanation: When a sentence is inverted with a prepositional phrase opening ('Among the documents...'), the real subject follows the verb. The subject here is the compound 'a forged certificate and two fake affidavits', which is plural and requires 'were'. Option A ('was') is wrong because it agrees only with the first noun, ignoring that compound subjects joined by 'and' need a plural verb.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'None of the evidence presented by the prosecution ___ sufficient to convict the accused'?

options.option_text: were — plural agreement with 'evidence', which is uncountable
are — present plural, wrong for an uncountable singular noun
was — correct; mass noun 'evidence' takes singular agreement
have been — present perfect plural, doubly incorrect here

questions.explanation: With 'none of the + uncountable noun', the verb agrees with the uncountable noun, which is grammatically singular. 'Evidence' is a mass noun, so 'was' is correct. Option A ('were') is the most tempting trap: students assume 'none' always signals plurality ('not any'), but the governing word here is the uncountable 'evidence', which overrides that impulse.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'She is one of those officials who ___ always punctual and detail-oriented at work'?

options.option_text: is — wrongly agrees with 'one' (singular) instead of 'officials'
was — past tense error; also incorrectly agrees with singular 'one'
are — correct; 'who' refers to plural 'officials', not to 'one'
has been — perfect tense unfit for a habitual general truth statement

questions.explanation: In the construction 'one of those [plural noun] who', the relative pronoun 'who' refers back to the plural noun 'officials', not to 'one'. The verb must therefore be plural: 'who are always punctual'. Option A ('is') represents the classic proximity error — agreeing with 'one' (the nearest singular) instead of the antecedent of the relative clause.

questions.stem: Select the correct verb form: 'Nearly sixty percent of the farmland in the northern districts ___ affected by the floods last season'?

options.option_text: were — plural agreement with 'districts', which is not the subject
have been — present perfect plural, wrong tense for a past event
are — present plural, wrong tense and number for this sentence
was — correct; 'percent of' agrees with 'farmland', an uncountable noun

questions.explanation: With 'percent of + noun', the verb agrees with the noun immediately after 'of'. 'Farmland' is uncountable (singular), so 'was' is correct. Option A ('were') is the dominant trap: the plural noun 'districts' appears nearby, causing students to choose a plural verb, but 'districts' belongs to a prepositional phrase and has no role as subject.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'Not only the principal but also the trustees ___ held accountable for the financial irregularities found in the audit'?

options.option_text: was — agrees with 'principal' (singular), ignoring the proximity rule for correlatives
is — present singular, wrong for both context and subject agreement
were — correct; with 'not only...but also', verb agrees with the nearest subject
had been — past perfect without a prior anchor event in this sentence

questions.explanation: With correlative conjunctions 'not only...but also', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it — here 'the trustees' (plural). Therefore 'were' is correct. Option A ('was') is the expected pitfall: students anchor on 'the principal' (the first element, singular) and pick a singular verb, violating the proximity rule that governs correlative pairs.

questions.stem: Choose the correct verb form: 'It is the labourers, and not the contractor, who ___ responsible for the persistent delay in project completion'?

options.option_text: is — proximity error; treats 'contractor' (singular) as the subject
are — correct; 'who' refers to 'the labourers' in this cleft structure
was — past tense, incorrect for a present-state cleft sentence
has been — perfect tense clashes with the simple present cleft context

questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence ('It is X who...'), 'who' refers back to X. Here X = 'the labourers' (plural), so the verb must be plural: 'who are responsible'. The phrase 'and not the contractor' is a parenthetical contrast that does not alter the grammatical subject. Option A ('is') is the high-frequency error: 'contractor' (singular) immediately precedes 'who', triggering a proximity-driven singular choice that is structurally incorrect.
